faqs.q: How do I know if the droppings in my Paterson basement are from rats?
faqs.a: Rat droppings are capsule-shaped and about half an inch long — much larger than mouse droppings — and they concentrate along walls, near food storage, and beside the grease-dark rub marks rats leave on the routes they run nightly. In Paterson's multi-families the signs gather in the cellar kitchens and around the old boiler rooms, and the run enters where the original coal-era openings were closed with whatever was at hand. A rat job here is three parts: trapping out the animals present, sealing the entries (a rat needs only a half-inch gap), and cutting the food and harborage that drew them. Any baiting, where it is used at all, follows New Jersey's pesticide rules.

faqs.q: How is the price for a Paterson wildlife job figured?
faqs.a: By what the inspection finds: one squirrel entry at a gable vent is a short visit, while a raccoon family plus chewed fascia and fouled insulation is several. A Hillcrest single with a squirrel-chewed gable and an Eastside three-family with a basement rat run are separated by building type as much as by animal, and the itemized quote is how an owner sees that cleanly. We walk the property with you, point out each opening, and price the removal, the sealing, and any cleanup as separate lines before work starts.

Paterson.wildlife_intro:
Paterson is New Jersey's silk city, dense with older housing around the Great Falls and the Passaic River: brick and frame multi-families in the Eastside and Totowa sections, older singles in Hillcrest, and mill-era blocks near downtown. Rats are the city's defining wildlife call, entrenched in the older basements, the shared laterals, and the blocks behind the food corridors. Raccoons den in the porch roofs and chimneys across the residential sections, squirrels work the Hillcrest canopy, and starlings and sparrows fill the vents and signs along Main and Market streets.

Attached housing changes the math. In a rowhouse or twin, one animal in a shared attic or party-wall void is every neighbor's problem, and sealing a single unit while the adjoining roofline stays open just moves the tenant sideways. We inspect the whole run of connected rooflines where access allows, coordinate timing with neighbors when entries cross property lines, and seal the full set of openings under one plan. Older masonry party walls hide voids that let squirrels travel between houses unseen — finding those routes is most of the job in attached stock. Paterson's multi-family rows share voids and runs, so entries are mapped across the connected buildings and quoted per owner, in the open.

faqs.q: Can you get a raccoon family out of a Clifton chimney?
faqs.a: Yes — spring raccoon mothers choose uncapped chimneys across Passaic County. Our crew checks whether pups are present before anything moves, removes the family together whenever we can, and fits a proper chimney cap so the same chimney is not a den again next spring.

faqs.q: We keep catching rats around our Passaic home — why do they come back?
faqs.a: Because the route and the restaurant are still open. Norway rats commute along fence lines, ivy, and utility runs, and they stay where trash, pet food, or a bird feeder feeds them every single night. Passaic rats run the fence and alley lines between buildings, and a single sealed house on an open block just hosts the overflow; the sanitation and entry work has to cover the property's full perimeter to hold. We map the runs, seal the building entries in metal and mortar — rats gnaw through foam and wood — and go over the sanitation changes that make the property stop paying out. Trapping alone, without those two halves, is a subscription, not a solution.

faqs.q: An opossum is living under my Passaic deck — should I be worried?
faqs.a: Mostly about the mess, not disease: opossums are not on New Jersey's high-risk rabies list, and they are placid, slow animals that would rather play dead than fight. River-side Passaic gives opossums a bank to live in and a row of crawlspaces to visit, and the calls concentrate in the houses whose vents face the water. They do shred insulation and vent ducts when they den in a crawlspace, so we take them out, clean up what they left, and screen the deck or crawlspace opening with buried hardware cloth. Check for young in the pouch season before assuming it is a solo tenant.

Passaic.wildlife_intro:
The city of Passaic is a dense, older mill city on its namesake river: multi-family homes and apartment buildings on a tight grid, the Main Avenue commercial spine, and the Dundee and riverfront edges where industry meets housing. Rats lead every list here, working the older basements, the alleys, and the blocks around the food businesses. Raccoons den in the flat and porch roofs, opossums commute along the river banks into the crawlspaces, and sparrows and starlings occupy the vents and cornices of the older buildings year-round.

Food decides where animals settle. Bird feeders spill seed that feeds rats at night, pet dishes sit out on porches, trash waits in cans a raccoon can open in seconds, and fallen fruit ferments under backyard trees. Removal without changing that menu is a short truce. We go over the property's food map with the homeowner — secured cans, feeders on baffled poles set away from the house, fruit picked up, grills cleaned — because the houses that stay quiet are the ones that stop advertising. The animal work and the housekeeping have to happen together. Passaic jobs pair the building sealing with the alley and dumpster audit, because on these blocks the food route is the rat route, and closing one without the other is half a job.

faqs.q: Why do I hear running in my Wayne Township ceiling every morning?
faqs.a: Daytime running, especially at dawn and mid-afternoon, points to gray squirrels — they commute. In Preakness and Mountain View the morning running usually enters at the dormer cheeks, where the subdivisions' repeated roof designs repeat the same weak joint. A squirrel entry is usually a gnawed widening at a gable vent, dormer cheek, or eave return, and the repair has to replace the chewed wood and back it with metal, or the next squirrel reopens it in days. One-way doors let the animals leave on their own schedule; then the opening is closed for good.

faqs.q: A groundhog is burrowing under my Wayne Township foundation — how bad is that?
faqs.a: Worse than it looks. A groundhog burrow system runs many feet with several chambers, and soil removed from under a slab or footing leaves voids that crack concrete and channel water against the foundation. Wayne's riverbank lots give groundhogs soft, banked ground above the flood line, and a burrow there can undermine a deck footing while looking like nothing from the yard. We trap at the active entrances, then backfill and screen the site so the next groundhog inherits a closed burrow. Groundhogs are on New Jersey's rabies-vector list — one more reason not to corner one yourself.

Wayne Township.wildlife_intro:
Wayne is Passaic County's big suburb: lake communities at Packanack and Pines Lake, postwar and newer subdivisions in Mountain View and Preakness, and the Passaic River floodplain threading its east side, with Ramapo foothills rising in the west. Squirrels and raccoons work the canopy subdivisions, groundhogs dig the field and riverbank lots, skunks and opossums are lake-community regulars, and bats take the attics near the woods and water. The river streets flood, and every flood season rearranges the ground-level entries on those blocks.

Storms open houses. Wind lifts shingles and ridge caps, ice works at eave flashing, and a single hard season can hand squirrels and raccoons three new doors into an attic that was tight for a decade. After major weather we check the roofline the way a roofer would — ridge, valleys, eave returns, plumbing stacks — because animal entries and water entries are usually the same gaps. Sealing done alongside sound roof repair lasts; sealing done over rotted, water-softened wood does not, and we will say which situation a house is in before any work is quoted. Wayne's river streets get a post-flood entry check as a standing recommendation, because high water moves soil, screens, and debris in ways that reopen sealed ground-level gaps.

faqs.q: I found a snake in my West Milford Township yard — could it be venomous?
faqs.a: Possibly, in this part of New Jersey, which is why identification comes before everything. The northern copperhead (state-Threatened) favors rocky, wooded slopes here, and the timber rattlesnake (state-Endangered) holds on along the ridges; both are left strictly alone and referred to NJ Fish & Wildlife's Venomous Snake Response Team. West Milford's ridges are among the few places in the state where a timber rattlesnake on a sunny rock is a plausible sighting, and the rule here is simple: admire it from distance and let the Response Team do any moving. Most calls turn out to be harmless black rat snakes or garter snakes, which we can catch and release outdoors within 200 meters, as state policy allows.

faqs.q: I found bat droppings in my West Milford Township attic — what happens next?
faqs.a: First we confirm the colony's size and find every entry, which is usually a cluster of small gaps at the ridge, a gable vent, or lifted flashing rather than one obvious hole. A converted lake cottage attic, low, hot, and undisturbed for weeks at a time, is nearly perfect bat housing, and droppings at the eave line are usually the first report. Exclusion happens inside the NJ Fish & Wildlife guideline windows — April 1 to May 14 or August 1 to October 15 — using one-way exits, and the guano cleanup afterward is handled as a health material, bagged out rather than swept into the air.

West Milford Township.wildlife_intro:
West Milford is Passaic County's wilderness township: Greenwood Lake and Upper Greenwood Lake at the north, the Wanaque watershed reservoirs fenced through the middle, and miles of rocky, forested ridges in between, with lake cottages and rural homes scattered along the shores and ridges. Raccoons and bats work the cottages and year-round homes, skunks and groundhogs take the clearings, and the rocky highlands are rattlesnake and copperhead country that residents share carefully. Many homes sit empty between weekends, and the animals keep their own schedule.

Empty houses invite quiet tenants. A home closed for the winter gives raccoons and bats months of undisturbed tenure, and the damage is usually discovered in a single bad hour at spring opening: fouled insulation, stained ceilings, a chimney full of nesting. Pre-closing walk-throughs in the fall — caps checked, vents screened, gaps at the waterline and roofline sealed — cost far less than post-winter remediation. For owners who are away, a neighbor or caretaker holding a key is the next best thing; small leaks and small entries both grow in an empty house. West Milford's part-time houses get a closing checklist written for the lake schedule: caps, vents, and the under-deck voids checked before the house goes quiet, not after it wakes up damaged.

faqs.q: What should I do about a skunk under my Hawthorne porch?
faqs.a: Keep dogs inside after dusk and do not block the opening yourself — a skunk sealed in will spray, dig, or die under the porch, and all three are worse than the skunk. Brook-side Hawthorne porches are skunk addresses by February in most years, and the same few streets call each season until the screening goes in. We take skunks out with covered, low-stress handling, then trench and screen the porch perimeter with buried hardware cloth so the next one cannot move in. Skunks are a New Jersey rabies-vector species, so distance and calm are the whole technique.

faqs.q: Do you charge to inspect a Hawthorne attic?
faqs.a: The inspection is the working visit: roofline, attic, and foundation get checked, entries get photographed, and you receive a written quote for the full job. Hawthorne inspections cover the brook-side foundation wall in full, because on these lots the water-facing side of the house is where the entries concentrate. That sequence — inspect first, quote in writing, then remove and seal — is how every job here runs, so there are no surprise line items after the animals are already out.

Hawthorne.wildlife_intro:
Hawthorne is a small, settled borough between the Passaic River and Goffle Brook: older colonials and capes on quiet streets, a compact downtown along Lafayette Avenue, and the brook park cutting through the middle. The water on two sides keeps the borough stocked. Raccoons commute from the brook corridor into the chimneys, squirrels work the mature street trees into the eaves, skunks dig the lawns near the water, and rats appear along the river-side and commercial edges. It is a borough where a house is rarely more than a few streets from a green corridor.

Decks and porches fail at ground level. The gap beneath a low deck is dark, dry, and sheltered enough for skunks, opossums, and groundhogs to den in, and lattice alone stops none of them. Lasting work means trenching around the structure and burying galvanized hardware cloth in an L-shape, so an animal digging at the edge meets mesh angled outward underground. Lattice or skirting goes back over the top for looks. It is unglamorous digging, and it is the difference between a den that stays empty and one that fills again every spring. Hawthorne's porches sit low and close to damp brook-side ground, and screening those voids is the borough's most repeated and most effective single job.
